newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Southcorp urges strategy from govt.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Southcorp urges strategy from govt.

text.p: Southcorp Holdings Ltd managing director Graham Kraehe said on Thursday the federal government needed to define its long-term industry policy as ad hoc and inconsistent decisions were sending out conflicting signals.

Speaking at an economic forum in Adelaide, Kraehe added his voice to calls for the adoption of a broadbased consumption tax, saying the government's failure to acknowledge the urgency of tax reform had been "extremely shortsighted".

In his criticism of government decisions, he highlighted the abolition of the tariff concession and DIFF (Development Import Finance Facility) schemes and reductions in the research and development tax concession and export development schemes.

"Cutbacks in these various business programmes have been taken for short-term budgetary savings, with little consideration for the longer-term benefits or of the signal it sends to potential investors in Australia," Kraehe said.

Kraehe said that while business applauded the government's labour market reform, tight fiscal policy and tariff reductions, there was a view that outside these areas the government was not spelling out a clear direction for the country.

"As a result, we have ad hoc policies which lack consistency between various departments at the federal level and between the federal and State policy," he told the Committee for the Economic Development of Australia (CEDA) forum.
"This lack of a consistent policy framework sends conflicting signals to business and potential investors in Australia," Kraehe said.

Kraehe said the challenges facing Australia included its ability to deal with excessive national wage claims, the need to overhaul the taxation system which "totally antiquated and overloaded with high compliance costs".
Another major challenge was continuing high unemployment and a long-term national growth rate of 3.5 percent a year was not enough to lower unemployment substantially, he said.
